content.statement: Styling a <div> with a large, bold font makes screen readers announce it as a heading.

remember: Meaning comes from the element, not its looks: use h1 to h6 for headings so screen readers and search engines see them.

content.prompt: A "View profile" control takes the user to the page /users/42. Which element fits best?

remember: Use a link (<a href>) for navigation to another page and a <button> for an action on the current page.

content.prompt: Three of these elements tell browsers and screen readers what their content is. Which one carries no meaning of its own?

remember: <div> and <span> are generic boxes; reach for a semantic element first and use them only when nothing fits.

content.prompt: Match each element with the content it is meant for.

right.text: Content only loosely related to what is around it, such as a sidebar
The primary content of the page, once per page
A block of major navigation links
A self-contained piece that makes sense on its own, such as a blog post

remember: main, nav, article and aside describe the role of a region, so assistive technology can list and jump between them.

content.prompt: Clicking Cancel closes the dialog, but the profile is saved anyway. Find the bug.
content.code:
<form action="/profile" method="post">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name">
  <button>Save</button>
  <button onclick="closeDialog()">Cancel</button>
</form>

fixes.text: Add type="button" to the Cancel button
Add type="submit" to the Save button
Change onclick to onsubmit on the Cancel button

remember: A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit"; give buttons that should not submit type="button".

content.statement: With the default box-sizing: content-box, padding and border are added on top of the width you set.

remember: content-box sizes only the content; the box on screen is width plus padding plus border.

content.prompt: You want more space inside a button, between its text and its border, filled with the button's background color. Which property do you change?

remember: Padding is space inside the border and shows the background; margin is transparent space outside it.

content.prompt: box-sizing is left at its default. How wide is .card from the outer edge of its left border to the outer edge of its right border?

remember: With content-box the visible width is width + left and right padding + left and right border; margin lies outside.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so two .col elements fit side by side in one .row, each exactly half of it, padding included.

remember: box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, so width: 50% stays half even with padding.

content.prompt: Two paragraphs sit one above the other in normal block flow. How much vertical space is between them?
content.code:
First

Second

remember: Vertical margins of adjacent blocks collapse to the larger of the two; margins of flex and grid items do not collapse.

content.statement: A class selector beats an ID selector as long as the class rule comes later in the stylesheet.

remember: Source order only breaks ties; a higher specificity wins wherever it appears in the file.

content.prompt: Which selector has the highest specificity?

remember: One ID outweighs any number of classes, and one class outweighs any number of element selectors.

content.prompt: What color is the text of the paragraph?
content.code: Hello

remember: An ID selector beats any number of classes, regardless of which rule comes last.

content.prompt: Inside <nav id="sidebar">, the link with class="active" turns bold but stays gray instead of crimson. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Change .active to a.active
Change .active to #sidebar a.active
Move the .active rule above #sidebar a

remember: A lone class cannot beat a selector with an ID; raise the override to at least the same specificity, such as #sidebar a.active.

content.prompt: Match each selector with its specificity, written as (IDs, classes, elements).

remember: :is() counts as its most specific argument, :where() always counts zero, and a pseudo-element counts like an element.

content.statement: Flexbox is designed to place items in rows and columns at the same time, like a table.

remember: Flexbox lays items out along one axis at a time; grid controls rows and columns together.

content.prompt: You are building a photo gallery whose rows and columns must line up in both directions. Which layout fits best?

remember: Use grid when items must align in two dimensions; flexbox is for a single row or column.

content.prompt: In a flex container with flex-direction: row, match each declaration with its effect.

right.text: Lets items move onto a new line when they do not fit
Adds space between items, but not at the outer edges
Centers the items horizontally, along the main axis
Centers the items vertically, along the cross axis

remember: justify-content works along the main axis, align-items across it; wrap allows new lines and gap spaces items apart.

content.prompt: .row contains .a, .b and .c, each with a single short word and no padding, border or margin. How wide is .c?

remember: flex-grow shares out only the leftover space: here 300px split 1:1:2 on top of each 100px basis.

content.prompt: The long line of code in the <pre> should scroll inside .main. Instead .main grows and the whole page scrolls sideways. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add flex-shrink: 1 to .main
Add min-width: 0 to .main
Change .sidebar to flex: 0 1 240px

remember: Flex items default to min-width: auto and will not shrink below their content; min-width: 0 lets the overflow happen inside them.

content.statement: In a mobile-first stylesheet, the base styles target small screens and min-width media queries add changes for wider ones.

remember: Mobile-first starts with the smallest layout and layers on wider ones with min-width queries.

content.prompt: A page has media queries for phones, but on a real phone it shows a tiny, zoomed-out desktop layout and none of the phone styles apply. What is most likely missing?

options.text: An @media screen block wrapped around all the styles
rem units instead of px in the media queries
A <!doctype html> line at the top of the page

remember: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers lay the page out at a wide desktop width and shrink it, so phone media queries never match.

content.prompt: An element is a direct child of <body>. Three of these widths shrink when the browser window gets narrower. Which one stays the same?

remember: % and vw follow the container and the viewport; rem follows the root font size, not the window.

content.prompt: The viewport is 1200px wide. What font-size does the h1 get?

remember: Media queries add no specificity; when several match, the later rule wins, so min-width queries must go from small to large.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the action buttons stay hidden until hover only on devices whose main input can hover; on touch screens they are always visible.

remember: Screen size says nothing about the input device; wrap hover-only effects in @media (hover: hover).

content.statement: Reading el.offsetHeight right after changing an element's style can force the browser to calculate layout immediately.

remember: Layout reads such as offsetHeight need up-to-date geometry, so after a style change the browser must lay out the page on the spot.

content.prompt: What does the browser do during layout, also called reflow?

options.text: Draws the pixels: text, colors, borders and shadows
Calculates the size and position of each affected element
Parses the HTML into the DOM tree
Downloads and runs the page's scripts

remember: Layout works out geometry; painting draws pixels afterwards.

content.prompt: JavaScript adds a class that changes an element's width. Put the browser's work for the next frame in order.

steps.text: Recalculate styles
Paint: draw the pixels into layers
Composite the layers onto the screen
JavaScript changes the class
Layout: compute sizes and positions

remember: A frame goes style, layout, paint, composite; a change that skips layout, such as transform, is cheaper.

content.prompt: A script has just changed el.style.height. Three of these reads force the browser to run layout right away. Which one does not?

remember: el.style only returns the inline style string; client*, offset*, scroll* and getBoundingClientRect() need fresh layout.

content.prompt: With 1,000 cards, resizeCards freezes the page, and the profiler shows a forced layout for every card. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use card.clientWidth instead of card.offsetWidth
Run the for loop inside requestAnimationFrame
Read every width in one loop, then set the widths in a second loop

remember: Alternating style writes and layout reads forces a layout per iteration; batch all reads first, then all writes.

content.statement: A click on a <button> inside a <div> also triggers a click listener on the <div>, unless propagation is stopped.

remember: Events bubble from the target up through every ancestor, which is what makes delegation possible.

content.prompt: What is event delegation?

options.text: Passing an event from one listener to another with dispatchEvent
One listener on a parent handles events from many children, using event.target
Adding a separate listener to every child element
Letting the browser decide which listener runs first

remember: Delegation puts one listener on a common ancestor; it also works for children added later.

content.prompt: A user clicks a submit button inside a form, and no listener calls preventDefault(). Put what happens in order.

steps.text: Listeners on the button itself run
The browser submits the form (the default action)
Capture listeners on the button's ancestors run, from window down
Bubbling listeners on the ancestors run, from the form up to window

remember: An event goes down in the capture phase, hits the target, bubbles up, and only then the default action runs, which is why preventDefault() can cancel it.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so a click anywhere inside a row, including on the <b> or <i>, opens that user.

remember: event.target is the innermost element clicked; target.closest(selector) walks up to the item the click belongs to.

content.prompt: Why does registering a touchstart or wheel listener with { passive: true } make scrolling smoother?

options.text: Passive listeners run in a Web Worker, off the main thread
Passive listeners are called at most once per animation frame
Passive listeners skip the bubbling phase, so fewer listeners run
The browser can scroll at once instead of waiting to see whether the listener calls preventDefault()

remember: A passive listener promises not to call preventDefault(), so scrolling does not have to wait for JavaScript.

content.statement: Changing a plain local variable (let count = 0) inside a React component makes the component re-render.

remember: Only state and props changes trigger a re-render; a local variable is also reset on every render.

content.prompt: A component keeps firstName and lastName in state and needs fullName for display. What is the best approach?

options.text: Keep fullName in its own useState and update it in a useEffect
Keep fullName in a useRef and update it in the change handlers
Keep fullName in a module-level variable outside the component
Compute it while rendering: const fullName = firstName + " " + lastName

remember: If a value can be computed from props or state, compute it during render instead of storing a second copy.

content.prompt: The button shows 0. What does it show after one click?

remember: count is a snapshot of this render; to apply several updates in a row, use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1).

content.prompt: Clicking "Sort by name" does not change the order on screen, although logging users shows them sorted. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Sort a copy: const sorted = [...users].sort(byName);
Pass an updater instead: setUsers(() => sorted);
Compare with a.name > b.name in byName

remember: sort() changes the array in place and returns the same reference, so React sees no change; sort a copy and set that.

content.prompt: A click handler calls setCount(1) and then logs "done". Put what happens in order.

steps.text: React calls the component function again with count = 1
The handler logs "done" and finishes
React updates only the DOM nodes that changed
React queues the state update
React compares the new JSX with the previous output

remember: setState only queues an update; React re-renders after the handler, compares the result and then commits the changes to the DOM.

content.statement: A useEffect callback runs after React has rendered the component and updated the DOM.

remember: Effects run after the commit, so they can safely touch the DOM or start subscriptions.

content.prompt: When does an effect run if you pass no dependency array at all?

options.text: Only when one of the props changes

remember: No array means after every render, [] means after mount only, and [a, b] means whenever a or b changes.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the timer stops when the component unmounts.

remember: Return a cleanup function from the effect; React calls it before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts.

content.prompt: Chat logs "render" in its body and has an effect with [roomId] that logs "connect" and returns a cleanup that logs "disconnect". It mounts with room a, then re-renders with room b (no Strict Mode). Put the logs in order.

steps.text: connect b
render a
disconnect a
render b
connect a

remember: When a dependency changes, React renders first, then runs the old effect's cleanup, then the new effect.

content.prompt: Switching the roomId prop from "general" to "random" changes nothing: the chat stays connected to "general". Find the bug.

fixes.text: Call conn.connect() before conn.on(...)
Remove the cleanup on line 10
Change [] to [roomId]

remember: Every prop or state value an effect reads belongs in its dependency array, or the effect keeps using the first value.

content.statement: A key only has to be unique among the siblings in the same list, not across the whole page.

remember: Keys are compared only within one list, so two different lists may reuse the same ids.

content.prompt: Why does React ask for a key on each element rendered from an array?

options.text: To set the HTML id attribute of each element
To sort the items in the order of their keys
To match each item with its previous render when the list changes
To let CSS select items by their key

remember: Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so it keeps, moves or removes the right elements.

content.prompt: Products from the API are rendered with products.map(...). Three of these are good keys. Which one is not?

remember: A key must stay the same between renders; Math.random() gives every item a new identity, so React remounts all of them.

content.prompt: EditForm keeps the typed draft in its own state. Fill the blank so the form starts fresh whenever a different user is shown.

remember: Changing a component's key makes React treat it as a new component, which resets all its state.

content.prompt: The user types "a" in the Milk row's input and "b" in the Eggs row's input, then clicks x in the Milk row. What is on screen?

options.text: One row: Eggs, with "b" in its input
One row: Eggs, with "a" in its input
One row: Milk, with "a" in its input
One row: Eggs, with an empty input

remember: With index keys, removing an item shifts identities, so DOM state such as typed text stays with the wrong row; key by a stable id.

content.statement: Wrapping every component in React.memo always makes an app faster.

remember: memo adds a props comparison to every render; it only pays off when re-rendering is costly and the props usually stay equal.

content.prompt: When does a component wrapped in React.memo skip re-rendering after its parent re-renders?

options.text: When the props have the same JSON content as before (a deep comparison)
When its own state has not changed, whatever the props are
When every prop is equal to its previous value by Object.is (a shallow comparison)
Never: memo only caches the component's code

remember: memo compares each prop shallowly; a new object, array or function created during the parent's render counts as changed.

content.prompt: Match each React API with what it does.

right.text: Caches a computed value until a dependency changes
Keeps the same function between renders until a dependency changes
Loads a component's code on its first render, from a dynamic import
Skips re-rendering a component when its props are unchanged

remember: memo skips renders, useMemo caches values, useCallback caches functions, and lazy defers loading code.

content.prompt: Not in Strict Mode. After the first render, the user clicks the button once. What is logged by the click?

options.text: render A, render B, render C

remember: An object literal in JSX is a new object on every render, which defeats memo; keep it outside the component or in useMemo.

content.prompt: Chart is defined as lazy(() => import("./Chart")) and rendered inside <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}> once showChart is true. Its code has not been loaded yet. Put what happens after the user clicks Show chart in order.

steps.text: The Spinner fallback appears on screen
setShowChart(true) queues a re-render
Chart replaces the Spinner on screen
The Chart code arrives and its module is evaluated
React renders Chart for the first time, which starts the import()

remember: lazy() starts the download on the first render, Suspense shows the fallback while it loads, then React renders the real component.

content.statement: A placeholder inside an input is a good replacement for a visible <label>.

remember: Placeholders disappear while typing and are not a reliable accessible name; give every input a real label.

content.prompt: What should the alt attribute of an informative image contain?

options.text: The image's file name, such as hero-banner.jpg
A short description of what the image shows or does, for people who cannot see it
Keywords that help search engines rank the page
A tooltip that appears when the mouse hovers over it

remember: alt text replaces the image for screen reader users; describe its purpose, and use alt="" for purely decorative images.

content.prompt: Match each piece of markup with what it is for.

right.text: Tells screen readers which language to pronounce the page in
Text read instead of the image
Ties visible text to a form field; clicking it focuses the field
Names a control that has no visible text, such as an icon button

remember: alt describes images, label names form fields, aria-label names icon-only controls, and lang sets the pronunciation.

content.prompt: Keyboard users report that they cannot see which button is selected when they press Tab. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add outline-offset: 2px to the rule
Replace outline: none with a visible outline, such as 2px solid
Add tabindex="0" to every button

remember: Never remove the focus outline without a visible replacement; keyboard users rely on it to know where they are.

content.prompt: Three of these can be reached with the Tab key without any extra attributes. Which one cannot?

remember: An <a> without href is neither focusable nor announced as a link; use <a href> to navigate and <button> for actions.

content.statement: Choosing <h4> instead of <h2> is the right way to make a section heading look smaller.

remember: Pick heading levels by the page outline, not by size; change how a heading looks with CSS.

content.prompt: A recipe lists its preparation steps, and their order matters. Which markup fits best?

remember: Use <ol> when the order of the items matters and <ul> when it does not; screen readers announce a list and how many items it has.

content.prompt: An orders table has a header row: Date, Customer, Total. Which header cell markup lets screen readers announce the column name with each data cell?

remember: Mark header cells with <th> so screen readers can read the matching column or row header along with each data cell.

content.prompt: Three of these inputs tell the browser what kind of value to expect, so a phone shows a fitting keyboard. Which one does not?

remember: type, not name, tells the browser what a field holds; email, tel and number get fitting phone keyboards, while name only labels the sent value.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so screen readers announce "Shipping speed" as the name of the radio group when the user tabs into it.
content.code:
<fieldset>
  ____
  <label>
    <input type="radio" name="ship" value="std"> Standard
  </label>
  <label>
    <input type="radio" name="ship" value="exp"> Express
  </label>
</fieldset>

remember: A group of radios or checkboxes gets its name from the <legend> of its <fieldset>; a heading or a stray label inside does not name the group.

content.prompt: What does this log in a browser?
content.code:
<label id="l">
  <input type="checkbox" id="c"> Remember me
</label>
<script>
  let n = 0;
  l.addEventListener("click", () => n++);
  l.click();
  console.log(n, c.checked);
</script>

remember: Clicking a label also clicks its control, and that second click bubbles back up, so a listener on a wrapping label runs twice.

content.prompt: The dialog is opened with showModal(). Cancel and Delete should close it and leave the choice in returnValue, without leaving the page. Instead the page reloads. Find the bug.
content.code: Delete this file?

fixes.text: Add type="button" to the Cancel and Delete buttons
Change method="post" to method="dialog"
Remove the method attribute so the form uses its default

remember: A <form method="dialog"> closes its <dialog> on submit and stores the button's value in returnValue instead of sending a request.

content.prompt: Match each piece of markup with how browsers expose it to screen readers.

right.text: No landmark role, a generic container
Contentinfo landmark
Banner landmark
Region landmark named by its heading

remember: header and footer are page landmarks only outside article, aside, main, nav and section, and a section is a region only once it has a name.

content.prompt: In a browser, a form has a required text field, then submit buttons Save (name=action, value=save) and Delete. The field is filled in. The user presses Enter in it. Put what happens in order.

steps.text: submit fires on the form
click fires on the Save button
The request is sent with action=save
keydown fires on the text field
The browser validates the required field

remember: Enter in a field clicks the form's first submit button, so its click handlers run and its value is sent; validation and submit come after that click.

content.statement: If a stylesheet sets .panel { display: flex; }, then <div class="panel" hidden> is visible on the page.

remember: hidden works only through the browser's default display: none, so any author display rule beats it; add [hidden] { display: none !important; }.

content.statement: Like margin, padding accepts negative values, such as padding: -10px.

remember: Padding can never be negative and padding: -10px is ignored as invalid; only margins accept negative values.

content.prompt: How wide is the content area of .box, the part where its text goes?

remember: With border-box, width is measured to the outer border edge, so the content gets width minus padding and border on both sides.

content.prompt: Every element should use border-box, so each .card fills the 300px .sidebar exactly. Instead each card is 336px wide. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add !important after border-box
Change the selector html to *, *::before, *::after
Move box-sizing: border-box into the .sidebar rule

remember: box-sizing is not inherited, so setting it on html changes only html; put it on *, *::before, *::after to reach every element.

content.prompt: Match each padding shorthand with the padding it sets.

right.text: 10px top, 20px right, 30px bottom, 40px left
10px top, 20px left and right, 30px bottom
10px on all four sides
10px top and bottom, 20px left and right

remember: Box shorthands go clockwise from the top, and a missing side copies its opposite: two values mean vertical, then horizontal.

content.prompt: None of these elements has a margin, and box-sizing is the default unless set. Order them from narrowest to widest on screen, border included.

steps.text: width: 250px; padding: 40px; box-sizing: border-box
width: 200px; padding: 30px
width: 240px; border: 10px solid; box-sizing: border-box
width: 220px; border: 5px solid

remember: Compare boxes by their border-box size: content-box adds padding and border to width, border-box already includes them.

content.statement: Under box-sizing: border-box, max-width: 600px caps the element at 600px including its padding and border.

remember: box-sizing also applies to min-width, max-width, min-height and max-height, not only to width and height.

content.prompt: .child is an empty block inside .parent, in normal flow. How tall is .child?

remember: Percentage padding on every side, top and bottom included, is a share of the containing block's width, not its height.

content.prompt: A plain inline <a> in the middle of a paragraph that wraps over several lines gets padding: 12px and a background color. What happens?

options.text: The line holding the link grows 24px taller to fit the padding
Top and bottom padding are dropped; only left and right apply
The link becomes an inline-block, so all padding takes up space
The background grows up and down, but line spacing stays the same

remember: Vertical padding on an inline element is painted but does not change the line height, so it can overlap the lines above and below.

content.prompt: An element has box-sizing: content-box, width: 200px, padding: 10px and a 1px border, and no scrollbar. Three of these include its padding. Which one does not?

remember: getComputedStyle(el).width reports the width property, here the content box; clientWidth adds padding, offsetWidth adds border too.

content.prompt: The h1's 48px top margin shows as a gap above .hero instead of inside its blue background. Fill the blank so the margin stays inside .hero without adding padding or a border.

remember: A first child's top margin collapses through a parent with no top padding or border; display: flow-root starts a new formatting context and stops it.

content.statement: Without any !important, a color set in an element's style attribute beats a color set by an ID selector in a stylesheet.

remember: A style attribute outranks every selector in the stylesheet, however specific; a stylesheet rule needs !important to beat it.

content.statement: The universal selector * adds as much specificity to a rule as a class selector does.

remember: The universal selector * counts zero, so even a plain element selector like p outranks a * rule.

content.prompt: The page links theme.css and then main.css. Both contain .btn { background: ... }, and theme.css finishes downloading last. Which background does a .btn get?

options.text: theme.css's, because the first rule for a property wins
main.css's, because its <link> comes later in the HTML
theme.css's, because it was the last file to finish loading
It varies between page loads, depending on network timing

remember: With equal specificity the later rule wins, and stylesheets count in document order, not in the order they download.

content.prompt: A shared stylesheet has .price { color: red !important; }. Inside <main id="checkout"> the prices must be green. Which change works?

options.text: style="color: green" on each price element
.price { color: green; } loaded after the shared file

remember: Normal declarations, even inline ones, never beat !important; you need another !important that wins on specificity or order.

content.prompt:
A

is styled by .note { color: blue; } at the end of the stylesheet. Three of these earlier rules still make it red. Which one does not?

remember: An attribute selector such as [class="note"] weighs the same as one class, so it ties with .note and the later rule wins.

content.prompt: Each <h2 class="title"> sits inside a <div class="card">. Fill the blank so titles become 18px on screens up to 600px wide.

remember: A media query adds no specificity; the rule inside must still match or beat the specificity of the rule it overrides.

content.prompt: What color is the word "world"?
content.code: Hello world

remember: Inherited values have no specificity: a rule that targets an element directly, even a bare p, beats what an #id parent passes down.

content.prompt: Every .btn except #submit gets a gray default that class rules like .btn.primary can override. A <button class="btn primary" id="save"> stays gray. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Change line 1 to .btn:not(:is(#submit))
Change line 1 to .btn:not([id="submit"])
Swap the order of the two rules

remember: :not() takes the specificity of its argument, so :not(#submit) adds a whole ID; [id="submit"] excludes the same button at class weight.

content.prompt:
Each pair sets color on

inside

; rules are unlayered unless stated. Match each pair with the cascade step that decides which rule wins.

left.text: #x p in layer base, p in a later layer

right.text: Cascade layers
Order of appearance
Importance
Specificity

remember: Among author rules the cascade compares importance, then layer, then specificity; source order only settles a full tie.

content.prompt:
Each of these sets color on the same

inside

, all written by the page author. Order them from lowest to highest priority.

steps.text: p { color: ... !important } in the stylesheet
style="color: ..." on the
style="color: ... !important" on the
#main p { color: ... } in the stylesheet
A running @keyframes animation of color

remember: Animations beat every normal declaration, inline ones included, but lose to !important; inline !important beats stylesheet !important.

content.statement: By default, display: flex lines up its children in a column, one below the other.

remember: The default flex-direction is row, so flex children sit side by side; flex-direction: column stacks them.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so .gallery has three columns of equal width.

remember: grid-template-columns lists one size per column; repeat(3, 1fr) is three columns that share the space equally.

content.prompt: .row holds four .item elements, each a single short word with no padding, border or margin. How wide is each .item?

options.text: 150px each; the fourth wraps to a new line
150px for three, 50px for the last one

remember: Flex items have flex-shrink: 1 and no wrapping by default, so a width is only a starting size they shrink from to fit.

content.prompt: A <ul class="menu"> holds three <li>, each with one <a>. The links should sit in one row, 16px apart, but they stack vertically. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add flex-direction: row to the .menu li rule
Move display: flex and gap from .menu li to .menu
Add display: flex to the .menu a rule

remember: display: flex arranges the direct children of the element it is set on, so put it on the parent whose children should line up.

content.prompt: A grid has grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr). Match each grid-column value with the columns the item covers.

right.text: Columns 2 and 3
Column 4 only
Columns 1 to 4
Two adjacent columns chosen by auto-placement

remember: grid-column numbers grid lines, not columns: 2 / 4 ends before line 4, negative lines count from the end, span sets only a length.

content.prompt: A flex container has flex-wrap: wrap. Put the browser's steps for sizing items along the main axis in order.

steps.text: Grow or shrink items to fill each line's free space
Find each item's flex basis, its starting size
Hand any space still left over to justify-content
Break the items into lines where they stop fitting

remember: Flexbox starts from the basis, wraps into lines, flexes each line, and justify-content only gets space that flex-grow left over.

content.statement: In a browser, a flex item with order: -1 is drawn first in its row, but the Tab key still reaches it in DOM order.

remember: order changes only where an item is drawn; keyboard focus and screen readers still follow the DOM, so keep meaningful order in the HTML.

content.prompt: This card grid is 1000px wide and looks right when full. When a search returns only two cards, each stretches to 500px. Which change keeps them 200px wide?

options.text: Change the max in minmax() from 1fr to auto

remember: auto-fit collapses empty tracks so the items stretch into the space; auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, so a few items stay track-sized.

content.prompt: How does a browser treat this grid-template-areas value?

options.text: nav covers the L-shaped group of three cells
nav keeps its top-left rectangle; the last cell is empty
The value is invalid, so the declaration is ignored
nav grows to its bounding box and overlaps main

remember: Every named grid area must be one rectangle; an L-shaped area makes the whole grid-template-areas value invalid, so it is dropped.

content.prompt: Three of these declarations do nothing on a flex item left at position: static. Which one still has an effect?

remember: Flex and grid items ignore float, clear and vertical-align, but z-index works on them even when position is static.

content.statement: Setting max-width: 100% on an image makes it stretch beyond its natural width to fill a wider container.

remember: max-width: 100% only shrinks an image to fit its container; it never enlarges it past its natural size.

content.prompt: A responsive page is open on a phone and the user turns the phone from portrait to landscape. The page does not reload. Put what happens in order.

steps.text: Styles from the queries that now match are applied
The page is laid out again and redrawn
The viewport becomes wider
The browser checks the media queries against the new size

remember: Media queries are live: when the viewport changes, the browser checks them again and restyles the page without a reload.

content.statement: On mobile browsers, an element with height: 100vh can be taller than the visible area while the address bar is showing.

remember: On mobile, 100vh is the height with the toolbars hidden; use 100dvh or 100svh when the element must fit the visible area.

content.prompt: On a phone, a data table with eight columns is wider than the screen and the whole page scrolls sideways. Which change keeps every column readable and stops the page itself from scrolling sideways?

options.text: Wrap the table in a <div> with overflow-x: auto

remember: A table cannot shrink below the width of its content; put it in a wrapper with overflow-x: auto so only the table scrolls.

content.prompt: At exactly 768px wide the nav is stacked like on mobile, but the menu button is hidden. Which change makes only one block apply at every width?

options.text: Write both conditions as only screen and (...)
Rewrite both queries with 48em instead of 768px

remember: min-width and max-width both include the boundary, so 768px matches both; end the lower range with width < 768px.

content.prompt: The viewport is 400px wide and <body> keeps its default 8px margin. Each rule styles a block inside <body>. Three make the page scroll sideways. Which one does not?

remember: An auto-width block fits its padding into the space; 100% plus padding, 100vw beside a margin and a min-width above max-width all overflow.

content.prompt: The same .card sits in a wide .main and a narrow .sidebar. Fill the blank so each card switches to flex by the width of its own column, while the columns stay as tall as their content.

remember: Container queries need an ancestor with container-type: inline-size; size also contains the height, so the box stops growing with its content.

content.prompt: The browser's default font size is 16px. What is the narrowest viewport width at which .nav is shown?

remember: em and rem in media queries use the browser's default font size, not the html rule, so 40em is 640px at the 16px default.

content.prompt: The script must always pick the same layout as the CSS @media (min-width: 768px). With a classic scrollbar, just above 768px the CSS shows desktop but the script says mobile. Find the bug.

fixes.text: return window.matchMedia("(min-width: 768px)").matches;
return document.body.clientWidth >= 768;
return screen.width >= 768;

remember: Media queries measure the viewport including the scrollbar but clientWidth leaves it out; use matchMedia so JS and CSS agree.

content.prompt: Match each piece of responsive image markup with what it does.

right.text: Tells the browser how wide the image will be drawn, before layout is done
Is used whenever its condition matches, e.g. to show a different crop
Offers files for different pixel densities at one fixed display size
Lists each file's real width so the browser picks by drawn size and density

remember: srcset only offers candidates and sizes says how wide the image will be drawn; use picture with source media when the choice must be forced.

content.statement: Hiding an element with visibility: hidden removes its box from the layout, so the elements after it move up.

remember: visibility: hidden keeps the element's space in the layout; display: none removes the box, so the content after it moves up.

content.prompt: Three of these CSS changes can resize or move elements, so the browser has to run layout again. Which one only needs a repaint?

remember: Geometry changes such as width, margin and font-size trigger layout; color only changes pixels, so the browser repaints without layout.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the hidden toast slides down out of view and the browser does not run layout on every frame of the transition.

remember: Animate transform or opacity to move things; animating bottom, margins or height makes the browser run layout on every frame.

content.prompt: In a browser, on a page with no stylesheets, what do the two console.log calls print?

remember: An element outside the document has no layout box, so offsetWidth is 0; after insertion the read lays it out and returns 250.

content.prompt: In a browser, .item has opacity: 0 and transition: opacity 300ms; .item.shown has opacity: 1. New items should fade in, but they appear at once. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add the shown class before calling list.append(li)
Read li.offsetWidth right before adding the shown class
Set li.style.opacity = "1" instead of adding the class

remember: A transition needs a computed start style; reading offsetWidth between insert and class change forces it, so the fade can run.

content.prompt: Match each task with the browser API built for it.

left.text: Run DOM writes right before the browser renders the next frame
Redraw a chart when its container changes size, without polling offsetWidth
Load images as they scroll into view, without reading positions on scroll
Build 500 rows off-document and insert them with one append

right.text: IntersectionObserver
DocumentFragment
requestAnimationFrame
ResizeObserver

remember: Observers report size and visibility changes without layout reads in hot handlers; rAF times writes to the frame; fragments batch inserts.

content.prompt: A class moves a card to a new spot in a grid. To animate the move with transform only, put the steps in order.

steps.text: Add the class, then read the card's new position
On the next frame, add a transition and remove the transform
Read the card's current position with getBoundingClientRect()
Set a transform that moves the card back to where it started

remember: FLIP: measure First, apply the Last layout and measure, Invert with a transform, then Play by transitioning the transform away.

content.statement: Reading el.innerText right after a style change can force a synchronous layout, while reading el.textContent does not.

remember: innerText depends on rendering, such as hidden elements and line breaks, so it needs fresh layout; textContent only reads the DOM text.

content.prompt: In a browser, .board has no padding or border and a zoom control has scaled it. What does this log?

remember: offsetWidth and the computed width give the layout size before transforms; getBoundingClientRect() returns the transformed box on screen.

content.prompt: In a browser, a ResizeObserver callback adds 1px to the width of the element it observes, every time it runs. What happens?

options.text: The callback re-runs within the same frame, forever, and the tab freezes
The width change is ignored, because styles set in the callback are discarded
The observer throws inside the callback and disconnects itself after one run
It runs once per frame, and each frame fires a ResizeObserver loop error event

remember: A ResizeObserver that resizes what it watches gets the new size next frame, and each frame fires a 'ResizeObserver loop' error event.

content.statement: Assigning button.onclick a second time keeps the first handler and adds the new one, just like addEventListener does.

remember: onclick holds one function, so a new assignment replaces the old one; addEventListener adds listeners side by side.

content.prompt: Match each part of the browser event API with what it does.

right.text: Stops the event from moving on to other elements
Detaches a listener that was added with that same function
The element the event started on, such as the clicked button
Cancels the browser's own action, such as following a link

remember: target is where the event started, preventDefault() cancels the default action and stopPropagation() ends the trip through the DOM.

content.prompt: A <button> is inside a <div>. Click listeners without capture were added in this order: div, button, document, button again. Put them in the order they run when the button is clicked.

steps.text: The div's listener
The button's second listener
The document listener
The button's first listener

remember: Listeners run element by element as the event bubbles up; on one element they run in the order they were added.

content.statement: In a click listener added to a <ul>, event.currentTarget is the <ul> even when the user clicked an <li> inside it.

remember: currentTarget is the element whose listener is running; target is where the event started, so delegation reads target.

content.prompt: In a browser, the user clicks the Buy button. What is logged?

remember: stopPropagation() keeps the event from other elements, but later listeners on the same element still run; stopImmediatePropagation() stops those too.

content.prompt: A dropdown closes from a bubbling click listener on document. A date picker on the page calls event.stopPropagation() on its clicks. With the dropdown open, the user clicks the date picker. What happens?

options.text: The dropdown stays open, because the click never reaches document
The dropdown closes, because listeners on document always run
The dropdown closes before the date picker's own listener runs
The dropdown stays open, and the date picker ignores the click too

remember: A stopPropagation() anywhere below hides the click from document-level "click outside" handlers; a capture listener on document still sees it.

content.prompt: Three of these events bubble, so one listener on a parent element sees them from every child. Which one does not bubble?

remember: mouseenter, mouseleave, focus and blur do not bubble; for delegation use mouseover, mouseout, focusin and focusout.

content.prompt: The cart listens on document. Fill the blank so the event fired on a normal button (no shadow DOM) reaches it.

remember: Events created with new Event() or new CustomEvent() do not bubble unless you pass bubbles: true, so ancestors never hear them.

content.prompt: In a browser, this script runs after the page, which has one <button>, has loaded. What does it log?

remember: btn.click() dispatches synchronously, so microtasks wait for the whole script; after a real user click they run between listeners.

content.prompt: The menu listens in the capture phase so no stopPropagation() can hide a click from it. After closeMenu() runs, clicks still call onOutside. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Pass { once: true } as the third argument
Pass true as the third argument, as when it was added
Call removeEventListener before setting menu.hidden

remember: removeEventListener must match the type, the function and the capture flag; a capture listener is only removed with capture: true.

content.statement: If a page renders the same Counter component twice, clicking one of them also changes the count shown by the other.

remember: Every rendered instance of a component gets its own state, so two Counters on one page count independently.

content.prompt: Which of these makes a React component re-render?

options.text: Assigning a new value to a ref's current property
Pushing an item into an array held in state
Calling its state setter with a different value
Changing a variable declared outside the component

remember: Calling a state setter with a new value schedules a re-render; refs, mutations and outside variables change silently.

content.prompt: Cart, email, todos and filter are already in state. Three of these should be computed during render. Which one needs its own state?

items.text: cartCount: how many items are in cart
canSubmit: whether email is not empty
query: the text typed in the search box
visibleTodos: the todos that match filter

remember: Store only what cannot be computed, like user input; counts, flags and filtered lists come from existing state during render.

content.prompt: Typing in the email input must update email without losing the name already stored in form. Fill the blank.

remember: A useState setter replaces the whole value instead of merging, so spread the old object into a new one and override the changed field.

content.prompt: The button shows 0. The user clicks it once. What does it show now?

remember: Queued updates run in order: an updater gets the pending value, while a plain value like count + 5 replaces it using this render's count.

content.prompt: The parent passes a new items array when a product is added. The item count updates, but the total keeps showing the first amount. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use a lazy initializer: useState(() => sumPrices(items))
Memoize it: useMemo(() => sumPrices(items), [])
Compute it each render: const total = sumPrices(items);

remember: useState uses its argument only on the first render; a value derived from props must be computed during render so it follows them.

content.prompt: Match each value with the best place to keep it in a React component.

left.text: Search text the user types, shown live in a heading
Interval id that a Stop button must clear later
Number of unchecked todos, with todos in state

right.text: A constant outside the component
A const computed during render
useState
useRef

remember: Use state for what the screen shows and changes, a ref for values that must not trigger renders, and compute anything derivable.

content.prompt: Summary keeps total in state and syncs it with useEffect(() => setTotal(sum(items)), [items]). The parent passes a new items array. Put what happens in order.

steps.text: The effect runs and calls setTotal with the new sum
React commits the new total to the DOM
Summary renders with the new items and the old total
Summary renders with the new items and the new total
React commits the old total to the DOM

remember: Syncing a derived value through an effect commits a stale value first and costs an extra render; compute it during render instead.

content.statement: In React, a component wrapped in memo still re-renders when a context value it reads with useContext changes, even if its props stay the same.

remember: memo only compares props; a component that reads a context with useContext re-renders whenever that context value changes.

content.prompt: The user clicks the counter up to 3, then types one letter in the input. The counter shows 0 again. Why?

options.text: A parent re-render always resets the state of its children
Each Page render creates a new Counter type, so React remounts it
useState(0) runs on every render and resets n to its initial value
Counter has no key, so React cannot match it with the last render

remember: Declare components at the top level; one defined inside another is a new type on every render, so React remounts it and loses its state.

content.statement: An effect with the dependency array [count] skips the first render and runs only when count changes later.

remember: An effect always runs after the first render; its dependency array only decides when it runs again.

content.prompt: UserList should load the users once when it mounts, but the browser keeps requesting /api/users in an endless loop. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Return the fetch promise from the effect
Pass [] as the second argument to useEffect
Start users as null instead of []

remember: Without a dependency array an effect runs after every render, so setting state inside it re-renders and runs it again in a loop.

content.prompt: Match each job in a React component with where its code belongs.

left.text: Load the profile whenever the userId prop changes
Listen to window resize while the component is mounted
Show the items filtered by the current search query
Send an order to the server when Buy is clicked

right.text: An effect with [] that returns a cleanup
No effect: compute it during render
No effect: do it in the click handler
An effect with [userId]

remember: Effects are for syncing with something outside React; derive values during render and handle user actions in event handlers.

content.prompt: Page starts with data = null and shows Loading... until data is set. Its effect with [] fetches and then calls setData(json). Put what happens in order.

steps.text: The effect runs and starts the fetch
Page renders again and shows the data
Page renders with data = null
The response arrives and setData(json) runs
React puts Loading... in the DOM

remember: An effect runs only after the first render is committed, so a fetch in an effect always shows the loading state first and the data on a later render.

content.statement: Under <StrictMode> in development, React runs each effect, then its cleanup, then the effect again on mount; production runs it once.

remember: Strict Mode remounts once in development to expose missing cleanups; an effect that cleans up correctly behaves the same either way.

content.prompt: userId changes from 1 to 2. The request for user 1 is slow and resolves after the one for user 2. What does the heading show in the end?

options.text: User 2's name: the effect for 2 ran last
Nothing: React ignores results of an old effect
User 1's name: its response arrived last
User 2's name: React aborts the first fetch

remember: React does not cancel async work when dependencies change; set an ignore flag in the cleanup so a late, stale response is dropped.

content.prompt: The timer shows 0, then 1, and then stays at 1 forever. Why?

options.text: The interval is cleared right after its first tick
React ignores state updates that come from a timer
setCount is async, so the later updates are dropped
Its callback still reads count from the first render

remember: A callback created in an effect with [] sees that render's values forever; use setCount(c => c + 1) or list count as a dependency.

content.prompt: Three of these keep the same identity for the whole life of a component, so as effect dependencies they never re-run the effect. Which one does not?

remember: React keeps useState setters, useReducer dispatch and useRef objects stable; a useCallback result changes whenever its own dependencies change.

content.prompt: The parent passes a new onMessage arrow on every render. Fill the blank so the chat reconnects only when roomId changes, yet each message reaches the latest onMessage.

remember: Keep a callback in a ref updated by an effect to call its latest version without listing it; a ref's .current never belongs in a dependency array.

content.prompt: Parent is rendered for the first time with createRoot, without Strict Mode. What does the console show?

options.text: parent layout, child layout, parent effect, child effect
child layout, parent layout, child effect, parent effect
child layout, child effect, parent layout, parent effect
parent layout, parent effect, child layout, child effect

remember: On mount React runs every layout effect before any passive effect, and in each pass a child's effects run before its parent's.

content.statement: A React component cannot read its own key: inside the component, props.key is undefined.

remember: React keeps the key for itself; if the component needs the id, pass it again as a normal prop such as id={item.id}.

content.prompt: In React, what happens when a list is rendered with items.map() but the items get no key?

options.text: Nothing renders and React throws an error
It renders, React warns and matches items by position
React silently gives each item a stable unique id
It renders, but every item remounts on each update

remember: Without keys React logs a warning and falls back to the index, so items are matched by their position in the list.

content.prompt: React warns that each child in the list should have a unique key. Where should key={u.id} go?

options.text: On the <ul> that wraps the list
On the <Users> element in its parent

remember: The key goes on the element map() returns, here <Row key={u.id} />; a key inside the child component comes too late.

content.prompt: Rows are keyed by index and each row keeps its own state, such as an expanded toggle. Three of these changes can show that state on the wrong item. Which one cannot?

items.text: Deleting an item from the middle
Adding a new item at the top
Adding a new item at the end

remember: Index keys only hold up while items never shift: appending is safe, but inserting, deleting or sorting moves state to other items.

content.prompt: Todos are created in the browser and rendered with key={t.id}. Fill the blank so every todo gets an id that no other todo will ever share.

remember: Give an item its id once, when it is created, from something that never repeats; todos.length repeats after a delete and text can repeat.

content.prompt: Not in Strict Mode. List first renders with names ["A", "B", "C"], then re-renders with ["C", "A", "D"]. What does the re-render log?

remember: An item whose key survives a reorder keeps its component; only removed keys unmount and new keys mount, and cleanups run first.

content.prompt: React warns that each child in the list should have a unique key, although every <dt> has one. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add key={t.id} to the <dd> as well, like the <dt>
Replace <>...</> with <Fragment key={t.id}>...</Fragment>
Move key={t.id} from the <dt> to the <dl> element

remember: The key belongs on the outermost element map() returns; to key a group of siblings use <Fragment key={...}>, since <> takes no key.

content.prompt: Each row keeps local state, such as an open toggle. Match each key with what goes wrong.

left.text: key={row.id + "-" + i}, and the list is re-sorted
key={i}, and the list is re-sorted
key={row.title}, and a row's title is edited
key={row.ownerId}, and one owner has several rows

right.text: State stays at its position and ends up on another row
The edited row remounts and its state resets
Updates can duplicate rows or leave removed ones on screen
Rows that change position remount and lose their state

remember: A key must be unique and never change for the same item; index parts, editable fields and shared values each break that.

content.prompt: Page renders <Profile key={userId} />, and Profile has a useEffect that returns a cleanup. Not in Strict Mode, userId changes from 1 to 2. Put what happens in order.

steps.text: The old Profile's effect cleanup runs
A new Profile renders, starting from its initial state
The new Profile's effect runs
Page re-renders and React sees that Profile's key changed
The old Profile's DOM is removed and the new one inserted

remember: A new key means a new instance: it renders fresh, the DOM is swapped, and only then does the old instance's cleanup run, before the new effect.

content.statement: In React, a keyed component that moves to a different parent element keeps its state, as long as its key stays the same.

remember: Keys are only compared among siblings of one parent; moving a component under another parent remounts it and resets its state.

content.statement: In JavaScript, import("./chart.js") returns a Promise that resolves to the module once it has loaded.

remember: import() loads a module on demand and returns a Promise for it; it is the building block of code splitting and React.lazy.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: A memoized function stores each result by its input and returns the stored result on a repeat call instead of computing it again.

content.prompt: Chart.jsx has only a named export, export function Chart(). Clicking Show should display the chart, but React throws an error instead. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Move the lazy() call inside Report, above useState
Use import("./Chart").then((m) => m.Chart)
Use import("./Chart").then((m) => ({ default: m.Chart }))

remember: lazy() needs a Promise for a module with a default export; for a named export, map it with .then((m) => ({ default: m.Chart })).

content.prompt: Chart only renders after a click on a Show chart button, and nothing else imports ./Chart. Match each way App.jsx loads it with when Chart's code is fetched.

left.text: import Chart from "./Chart"; at the top of App.jsx

right.text: When the pointer moves over the Show chart button
Together with App.jsx, before App can run
Soon after App first appears, before any click
When the click makes <Chart /> render for the first time

remember: A static import loads with its importer, lazy() loads on first render, and calling import() yourself (on hover or after mount) fetches earlier.

content.prompt: Parent keeps filter in state and renders memo(List) with items and filter. List filters items in useMemo with [items, filter]. Put what happens after filter changes from "a" to "ab" in order.

steps.text: useMemo sees that filter changed and runs the filtering again
React commits the new rows to the DOM
Parent re-renders and creates List's props with the new filter
List's function body starts running
memo compares List's old and new props and finds filter changed

remember: memo checks props before the child renders, useMemo checks its dependencies during that render, and the DOM changes only in the commit after.

content.statement: React.memo stops a component re-rendering when a context it reads with useContext changes, as long as its props stay equal.

remember: memo only compares props; a change in a context the component reads still re-renders it, even when every prop is equal.

content.prompt: Toolbar is wrapped in memo and receives onSave={handleSave}. Which expression for handleSave is a function that calls save(id) and stays the same until id changes?

remember: useMemo calls its function and caches the result, useCallback caches the function itself: useCallback(fn, deps) equals useMemo(() => fn, deps).

content.prompt: App loads Chart with lazy(() => import("./Chart")), yet the production build still puts Chart's code in the main bundle. Which of these explains it?

options.text: Chart is rendered on the first screen, so the bundler inlines it
A module in the main bundle statically imports a helper from ./Chart
The Suspense boundary sits above App instead of right around Chart
lazy() is called at module level, so it loads Chart as App.jsx runs

remember: A dynamic import only splits off a module that nothing imports statically; one static import from the main bundle pulls it back in.

content.prompt: Chart is wrapped in memo, and Parent re-renders because its own state changed. Each item is the only prop Chart gets. Three make Chart re-render anyway. Which one does not?

items.text: onSelect={setSelected}, a setter from Parent's useState
rows={rows.slice(0, 10)}, with rows from Parent's state
format={formatDate}, a function declared in Parent's body

remember: useState setters keep their identity across renders; JSX children, new arrays and functions declared in the body are new on every render.

content.prompt: Every fetch returns a new data object, but data.version changes only when the points change. Fill the blank so Chart re-renders only when the version changes.

remember: memo's comparison function returns true when the props count as equal so the render is skipped, the opposite of shouldComponentUpdate.

content.statement: Turning a form field's border red is enough on its own to tell every user that the field has an error.

remember: Never rely on color alone; pair it with text or an icon, because many users cannot tell red from other colors.

content.statement: A "Skip to main content" link lets keyboard users jump past the navigation that repeats at the top of every page.

remember: A skip link, usually the first focusable element, lets keyboard and screen reader users bypass menus repeated on every page.

content.prompt: A user clicks "Delete account" and a custom modal dialog opens over the page. Where should keyboard focus go when it opens?

options.text: Stay on the Delete account button behind the dialog
Go back to the first link at the top of the page
Move into the dialog, for example to its first button
Nowhere, because screen readers read new dialogs aloud

remember: When a modal opens, move focus into it; when it closes, send focus back to the control that opened it.

content.prompt:
Below a labelled password input,

At least 8 characters

appears. On focus, a screen reader reads only the input's label. What makes it read the error too?

options.text: Give the message tabindex="0" so users can Tab to it
Add aria-hidden="true" to the error message
Move the message above the input in the HTML

remember: aria-describedby points a field at the ids of hint or error text, which screen readers read after the field's label.

content.prompt: Three of these hide an element from screen readers as well as from sight. Which one only hides it visually?

remember: opacity: 0 only makes an element invisible; screen readers still read it and Tab still reaches its links and buttons.

content.prompt: The <nav> starts with the hidden attribute. Fill the blank so a screen reader tells the user whether the menu this button controls is currently open.

remember: A button that shows and hides a region sets aria-expanded to match; aria-pressed is for toggles like Bold, not for menus.

content.prompt: In a browser, what accessible name does a screen reader announce for this button?
content.code: invoice 42 Delete

remember: aria-labelledby beats aria-label, which beats the text inside; the referenced texts are joined in the order the ids are listed.

content.prompt: CSS slides the drawer off-screen when it loses the open class. After closeDrawer() runs, its links must be skipped by both the Tab key and screen readers. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Replace it with drawer.setAttribute("aria-disabled", "true")
Keep it and also set drawer.tabIndex = -1
Replace it with drawer.inert = true

remember: aria-hidden hides content from screen readers only, so its links stay in the Tab order; inert removes a subtree from both.

content.prompt: In a browser, match each focused element (not inside a form) with how the keyboard operates it.

left.text: <input type="radio"> in a group of three

right.text: Arrow keys move the choice; Tab moves past the group
Space activates it; Enter does not
Enter activates it; Space does not
Enter and Space both activate it

remember: Links fire on Enter, buttons on Enter and Space, checkboxes on Space; a custom role must copy the keys of the element it imitates.

content.prompt: These elements appear in the HTML in the order listed, and nothing else on the page can take focus. Put them in the order the Tab key visits them, starting from the top of the page.

steps.text: <input name="q">
Help
Card
<button tabindex="1">Save</button>
<button tabindex="2">Send</button>

remember: Positive tabindex values go first, lowest to highest and ties in DOM order, then everything else in DOM order; avoid them.
